paragraphs.paragraph_en: Recovering missing sensor observations is essential for reliable downstream monitoring in industrial and clinical time series. While diffusion-based imputation models generate plausible trajectories under random missingness, they suffer from high sampling latency and lose global periodic coherence when entire sensor blocks drop out consecutively. We present FlowImp, a conditional flow-matching framework that reconstructs contiguous missing blocks in three ODE solver steps. Specifically, FlowImp anchors straight transport paths on observed spectral priors and enforces cross-channel phase consistency via a lightweight Fourier regularizer. Across six multivariate benchmarks under 50% block missingness, FlowImp reduces imputation MAE by 19.3% compared with CSDI while accelerating inference by 24x.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: Multivariate time series forecasting underpins safety-critical scheduling across smart power grids, cloud clusters, and automated manufacturing. In these operational settings, control systems rely on multi-horizon predictions to balance supply fluctuations and prevent cascading overload. However, field sensors routinely operate under abrupt regime shifts, irregular sampling intervals, and high-frequency measurement noise. Failing to accommodate such non-stationary disturbances degrades long-range forecast reliability and triggers costly control oscillations.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: Recent deep forecasters have substantially reduced long-horizon error by replacing point-wise attention with sub-series patch tokenization and frequency-domain decomposition. These architectures effectively capture recurring seasonal patterns when training and test sequences share stationary statistical moments. Yet they implicitly assume that inter-channel correlations and spectral energy distributions remain time-invariant across the prediction window. When external shocks alter underlying system dynamics, this stationarity assumption collapses, causing frozen spectral filters to project outdated trends.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: Bridging non-stationary robustness and amplitude fidelity remains a core bottleneck in long-horizon forecasting. While instance normalization strips time-varying mean and variance shifts to stabilize attention weights, it simultaneously erases physical scale cues required to predict extreme load peaks. Conversely, retaining raw unnormalized inputs exposes self-attention layers to severe covariate shift, causing validation error to diverge over extended horizons. Resolving this tension requires a mechanism that disentangles intrinsic temporal dynamics from transient scale drift without discarding magnitude information.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: To resolve this dilemma, we propose DyTS-Net, a dual-stream forecasting architecture that decouples stationary structural modeling from dynamic scale trajectory estimation. Our key insight is that while high-frequency phase relationships benefit from normalized shift-invariant attention, macro-scale amplitude evolution follows a low-dimensional continuous dynamical system. Specifically, DyTS-Net first extracts scale-invariant temporal tokens via spectral patch attention, and concurrently models non-stationary mean-variance evolution through a lightweight neural ODE branch. Recombining both streams at the decoding stage preserves sharp peak magnitudes without sacrificing training stability.

(2) We propose DyTS-Net, a hybrid architecture that couples shift-invariant spectral attention with a continuous neural ODE scale tracker. (3) We demonstrate across eight public benchmarks and industrial wind-power telemetry that DyTS-Net lowers long-range MSE by up to 17.4% while cutting inference latency nearly in half.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: Consider a multivariate time series $\mathbf{X}_{1:L} = [x_1, \dots, x_L]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times C}$ recording $C$ correlated sensors over lookback horizon $L$. Given an binary observation mask $\mathbf{M} \in \{0, 1\}^{L \times C}$ indicating irregular sensor dropouts, our objective is to learn a generative mapping $p_\theta(\mathbf{Y}_{L+1:L+H} \mid \mathbf{X}_{1:L} \odot \mathbf{M})$ over future horizon $H$. Crucially, unlike standard settings that assume time-invariant marginal distributions, we explicitly account for non-stationary regime shifts where $\mathbb{E}[x_t]$ and $\text{Cov}(x_t)$ evolve continuously between the lookback and forecasting windows.

paragraphs.paragraph_en: Figure 2 illustrates the overall architecture of DyTS-Net, which maps raw sensor streams to multi-horizon forecasts through three sequential stages. Given an input sequence $\mathbf{X}$, the Adaptive De-stationary Tokenizer first separates local trend-scale statistics from normalized sub-series patches $\mathbf{Z}_0$. paragraphs.paragraph_en: Standard dot-product attention measures token similarity purely by instantaneous amplitude alignment, often matching noisy spikes across unrelated time steps. To enforce temporal coherence, we observe that genuine physical interactions between industrial sensors exhibit consistent phase lag across dominant frequencies. Formally, given query and key projections $Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, we modulate the attention logits via a phase-alignment mask: $\mathcal{A}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}} - \lambda \|\Delta \Phi_{Q,K}\|_1\big)V$, where $\Delta \Phi_{Q,K} \in [-\pi, \pi]^{N \times N}$ denotes the instantaneous Hilbert phase difference matrix and $\lambda > 0$ controls phase selectivity. Penalizing large phase discrepancies prevents spurious attention weights between out-of-phase noise bursts.

Compared with channel-independent PatchTST, DyTS-Net reduces average MSE by 14.2% on the 862-channel Traffic benchmark, where modeling spatial-temporal congestion propagation across adjacent road sensors is critical. Removing the neural-ODE scale tracker (w/o Scale-ODE) triggers the sharpest degradation during seasonal transition months on ETTm2, raising 720-step MSE by 19.4% as the decoder fails to track shifting baseline temperatures. paragraphs.paragraph_en: In this work, we resolved the long-standing tension between shift-invariant normalization and physical amplitude preservation in non-stationary time series forecasting. By decoupling frequency-domain phase attention from continuous neural-ODE scale tracking, DyTS-Net captures long-range seasonal dependencies while accurately reconstructing extreme peak magnitudes. Empirical evaluations across eight benchmarks and industrial wind-power telemetry demonstrated MSE reductions of up to 17.4% alongside a 45% reduction in computational overhead. Beyond forecasting, this structural-scale disentanglement principle provides a generalizable foundation for anomaly detection and closed-loop predictive control in non-stationary cyber-physical systems.
